top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: The extracted data were systematised via a specially constructed standardised data extraction form (see study protocol), and the extracted data were then reviewed for consistency by the reviewers. Each included study was independently reviewed for critical appraisal and bias reduction, and a modified version of the Newcastle Ottawa cohort scale was used for cross-­ sectional research (online supplemental file 1). 29 Consensus was used to settle disagreements; the results are shown in table 1. General study information, participant and intervention characteristics, withdrawal information and outcome information were extracted.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: A total of eight cross-­ sectional studies were included in the meta-­ analysis. We identified 3775 articles by searching the databases MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase (Ovid) and Web of Science. A total of 1456 studies were excluded because of duplication, while 1565 were classified as ineligible by automation tools. Another 546 studies were removed for additional reasons. We examined the titles and abstracts of 208 studies and excluded 157 on the basis of our findings. We screened 51 articles for eligibility. Eight studies were included in the meta-­ analysis. The PRISMA flow chart is shown in figure 1.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: A meta-­ analysis was also conducted to investigate the associations between MetS and MedDiet adherence. To determine the overall estimated OR and its related 95% CIs, the random-­ effects inverse variance model with the traditional DerSimonian and Laird method was used. To measure the percentage of disparities across studies, we used the inconsistency index ( I 2 ), which was calculated with the Cochran Q statistic. I 2 values of 0%-40%, 30%-60%, 50%-90% and 75%--100% were considered cut-­ off values for non-­ important, moderate, substantial and considerable degrees of inconsistency, respectively. 30

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.section: Results Of The Publication Bias Analysis
top_evidence.text: We could not observe any publication bias in these studies. The funnel plot was not asymmetrical, and Egger's test yielded a p value of 0.162 (figure 3).

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: The results of the individual studies are presented in figure 2. Children and adolescents with low adherence to the MedDiet had greater odds of developing MetS compared to those with medium to high adherence. The OR for this association was 2.18, with a 95% CI ranging from 1.45 to 3.28 ( p < 0.001). The inconsistency among the studies, as assessed by the I² statistic, was 64.15%.

Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: A sensitivity analysis was conducted by sequentially omitting one study at a time to assess the robustness of the overall effect estimate. The pooled ORs remained stable across all iterations, ranging from 1.91 to 2.43, and all remained statistically significant (p ≤ 0.001). These findings indicate that no single study unduly influenced the overall results, supporting the robustness of the association between low adherence to the MedDiet and higher odds of MetS in children and adolescents (figure 4).
